questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the client's actual goal is processing 3x current claim volume with the same staffing, at the same average cycle time — not new capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since AI projects should aim to create new capability.
Frame the architecture around efficiency, and build success metrics around throughput per headcount rather than novel capability.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction exclusively, regardless of what discovery surfaced.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since the system either works or it doesn't.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (more volume, same headcount, same cycle time) is a throughput/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A, C, and D either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Claims intake, triage, and adjudication each require different steps depending on the claim type, prior findings, and missing information discovered along the way.

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since the right steps vary by case and depend on intermediate findings.
A fixed workflow, since claims processing is a well-established business process.
An augmented LLM pattern, since a single enhanced call is sufficient for any insurance workflow.
Whichever pattern is fastest to implement, since the patterns are functionally interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by case and depend on intermediate findings are the defining case for an agentic pattern. B assumes a predictability the scenario explicitly lacks; C undersells the orchestration actually needed; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (document intake, fraud-signal analysis, coverage lookup, adjudication recommendation).

choices.text: Let each subagent communicate results directly to whichever subagent needs them next, to minimize hops.
Merge all four responsibilities into one subagent to avoid coordination overhead.
Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
Let subagents communicate directly, but log the traffic for later review.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. A and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; B discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition assigned only auto-claims to the pipeline — claims involving injury or third-party liability are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent specifically for edge cases.
Add a prompt instruction telling subagents to flag claims they don't recognize.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so they can handle any claim type.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers all claim categories, including injury and liability claims, rather than tuning the existing subagents.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole claim categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. A, C, and B all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The design must align technical architecture to a specific business value pillar the client actually cares about, distinct from a generic "we added AI" narrative.

choices.text: Efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and performance SLAs are examples of such pillars; the chosen one should drive both the architecture and its success metrics.
Any AI system inherently demonstrates transformation, so no further framing is needed.
Business value pillars are a sales concern, not an architectural one.
The pillar should be chosen after the system ships, based on whatever benefit is easiest to measure.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The client's claims adjuster team is skeptical of automation and worried about job security; discovery interviews surface this repeatedly.

choices.text: Ignore the sentiment since it's not a technical requirement.
Treat it as a real implicit constraint alongside the explicit technical requirements — it will shape adoption, rollout sequencing, and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter most.
Proceed with the technical design and let change management handle it separately with no architectural input.
Recommend against the project entirely based on the sentiment.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. A and C treat it as out of scope; D overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the technical case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why the fraud-signal subagent uses a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the document-intake subagent.

choices.text: "Higher tier because it's more important" is a sufficient answer.
Avoid explaining tier differences, since stakeholders don't need technical detail.
Explain the tradeoff explicitly: fraud-signal analysis needs deeper reasoning that justifies the added cost/latency, while document intake is simpler and better served by a faster, cheaper tier.
Use the same tier everywhere for simplicity, regardless of task difficulty.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. A and B withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The architecture's current design produces a final adjudication recommendation with no mechanism to learn from adjuster overrides or outcomes over time.

choices.text: Add a feedback loop capturing adjuster overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component, so the system can improve post-deployment.
This is acceptable since the initial design already reflects best practice.
Feedback loops are a data science concern unrelated to the architecture.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase with no current design hooks.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures adjuster overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment, per the input→processing→output→feedback loop framing. B, C, and D all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The client wants a single enhanced LLM call — with retrieval of policy documents — to answer straightforward coverage questions, without any multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: This calls for a full multi-agent architecture regardless of the simplicity of the task.
This cannot be built with Claude at all, since it doesn't involve an agent.
This requires a fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps.
An augmented LLM pattern (a single call enhanced with retrieval/tools) fits this simpler augmentation need without the overhead of agentic orchestration.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and C over-engineer a simple augmentation need; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The document-intake subagent's toolset has grown to include tools for tasks like customer notification and billing lookup that are unrelated to document intake.

choices.text: This has no architectural downside as long as the subagent's prompt is well-written.
This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; the unrelated tools should be removed or moved to a more appropriate subagent.
More tools always improve a subagent's flexibility and should be encouraged.
The fix is to increase the subagent's context window.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not just writing around it. A and C ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently processes each claim sequentially through document intake, fraud analysis, coverage lookup, and adjudication, even though fraud analysis and coverage lookup have no dependency on each other's output.

choices.text: Run fraud analysis and coverage lookup as independent, parallel subagent calls once document intake completes, rather than sequentially.
Sequential processing is required for auditability.
Parallelization is not possible with a coordinator/subagent architecture.
Combine fraud analysis and coverage lookup into a single subagent to avoid the sequencing question.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (document intake) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

Present the full technical architecture diagram with no simplification.
Describe input → processing → output → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against business outcomes, without requiring them to understand implementation internals.
Skip a high-level description and go directly into an implementation demo.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; B is too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely.

questions.prompt: A competing vendor proposes a single, generalist agent with all tools (document processing, fraud detection, coverage lookup, adjudication) rather than a coordinator with specialized subagents.

choices.text: A single generalist agent scales better as tool count grows.
Specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice with no reliability benefit.
There's no meaningful architectural difference between the two approaches.
A single agent holding every tool and responsibility is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents scoped to narrower roles.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. A, C, and B understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The claims architecture must eventually support a new claim type (parametric weather claims) the client is planning to launch next year, but detailed requirements aren't available yet.

choices.text: Ignore future claim types until requirements exist.
Design the current decomposition and tool/subagent boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements.
Build full support for parametric weather claims now, guessing at requirements.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase until the future requirements are finalized.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. B ignores a known future need entirely; C wastes effort guessing at undefined requirements; D blocks current delivery unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Claims-Processing Architecture (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: An insurance client wants to modernize claims intake, triage, and initial adjudication. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the client's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The steering committee wants documentation they can hand to a new engineering team in a year, who will extend the system without the original architect present.

choices.text: Document only the final configuration values, since implementation is self-explanatory.
Document the architecture and the reasoning ("why") behind key decisions — pattern choices, decomposition boundaries, tier selections — not just the final "what."
Rely on the original architect remaining available indefinitely instead of documenting.
Documentation is unnecessary if the code is well-organized.

questions.explanation: Documenting the reasoning behind key decisions, not just final values, is what lets a future team safely extend the system without the original architect present. A, C, and D all leave the actual knowledge transfer gap unaddressed.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most analyst questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many documents, and a small fraction are simple lookups.

choices.text: Use one fixed model tier for all questions, regardless of complexity.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.

Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for the deep multi-step cases.
Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and B ignore fit-to-task; D sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (analyst persona, citation requirements, formatting rules) followed by retrieved document excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.
Put retrieved content first since it's most relevant to the specific query.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce both latency and cost across the high query volume.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and B all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form filings (10-Ks, earnings call transcripts) with short structured data (a table of quarterly metrics).

choices.text: One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well.

Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
Structured data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Analyst queries range from exact lookups ("Q3 2026 revenue for Company X") to conceptual questions ("how has Company X's margin narrative evolved over the last four quarters").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and B force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Analysts need citations that reliably map each claim to a specific source document and page/section, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without further structure.
Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (document, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible source for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted documents at the end of each response.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved sources disagree on a company's reported Q3 revenue by a small margin — likely different reporting bases (GAAP vs. non-GAAP).

choices.text: Average the two figures and present the average.
Omit the revenue figure entirely since sources disagree.
Always prefer whichever source was retrieved first.
Present both figures explicitly annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely methodological explanation (e.g., GAAP vs. non-GAAP), rather than silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and likely methodological explanation preserves the actual information for the analyst rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. A, C, and B all discard or obscure a genuine data conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.
Post-process every response to strip leading text before the first `{`.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; D doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal research-notes system, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

choices.text: Hard-code the research-notes integration into this platform's application code only.
Paste the entire research-notes corpus into every prompt.
Build an MCP server exposing the research-notes operations as tools/resources, reusable across the multiple internal Claude-powered tools that need it.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, B, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full research-notes catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Progressive discovery (querying a catalog resource as needed) scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the corpus grows.
Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. B and C ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; D removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: An analyst asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved documents before concluding.

choices.text: A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-document synthesis question.
Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple documents regardless of prompting approach.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, disclaimer language, formatting rules) across several different analyst-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).
Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Modular prompts are the same thing as prompt caching.
Standardization across features isn't achievable with prompt design.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. B reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific figure from the correctly retrieved source document.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted figures against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C doesn't address correctness; B incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether analyst-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the research platform.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, C, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; B over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model, Prompting, and RAG Integration for a Financial Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: A financial research platform wants Claude to answer analyst questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of filings, earnings transcripts, and internal research notes. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved document excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, C, and B all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system answers customer questions directly to deflect support tickets. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only ticket-deflection rate and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Deflection rate alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — a system that deflects tickets but is too slow, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it deflects tickets. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)

A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. B, C, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.

This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)

Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a knowledge-base refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)

Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.
Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-topic or per-query-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. A and C accept a monitoring blind spot; B drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

Segment accuracy by topic and query type before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by topic/query type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

Check the escalation-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated deflection-rate improvement could be masking an increase in inappropriate deflections of complex cases.
False-positive escalation behavior is not something evaluation can measure.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated deflection-rate improvement could mask a worsened escalation failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)

Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.
Remove the policy document entirely to save tokens.
Apply prompt caching to the static policy document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.

Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and D accept the described dysfunction; C addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. B and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Production Support-Deflection System (Questions 31–45)

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment (Questions 46–60)

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved opinion excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long opinions, never for typical queries.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only forecast-adoption rate (how often reps accept the copilot's forecast) and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Adoption rate alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — a system that gets adopted but is too slow, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if adoption looks healthy. A, B, and C each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past forecasting scenarios.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves forecast quality before rolling it out to all revenue teams.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all teams immediately and monitor for problems.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Change the prompt and the underlying model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; C confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: A forecast is materially wrong. Investigation shows the underlying pipeline data (historical deal velocity, quota attainment) was correctly retrieved, and the model's narrative summary misinterpreted the trend direction.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the data pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (misinterpreting correctly retrieved data), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than pipeline changes.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.

questions.explanation: Correct pipeline retrieval plus a misinterpreted trend direction is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than pipeline or model-tier changes. A and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled CRM data-sync refresh, the copilot starts producing confident but incorrect quarterly forecasts, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Investigate the data pipeline/CRM-sync layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data-refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at the data pipeline/CRM-sync layer. B, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a scheduled data refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting forecast accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average forecast-accuracy score.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-segment or per-product-line breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and C accept a monitoring blind spot; D drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence forecasts by 75%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by product line and deal size before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by product line and deal size before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves forecast-adoption rate, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate at which the copilot overconfidently forecasts deals that later slip.

choices.text: Check the deal-slippage-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated adoption-rate improvement could be masking an increase in overconfident forecasts on deals that later fall through.
Adoption rate alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.
Deal-slippage failure behavior is not something evaluation can measure.

questions.explanation: An isolated adoption-rate improvement could mask a worsened deal-slippage failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. B and C ship without adequate testing; D incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of forecasts are numerically accurate but rated poorly by reps in feedback surveys.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves rep satisfaction.

Investigate a dimension beyond numerical accuracy — e.g., explanation clarity, actionability of the narrative, or tone — since "accurate but poorly rated" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Ignore rep satisfaction scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (explanation clarity, actionability, tone) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends full quarter-to-date deal history plus a large static forecasting-methodology document on every turn of a multi-turn coaching conversation.

choices.text: This has no optimization opportunity since full history is always required.
Remove the methodology document entirely to save tokens.
Apply prompt caching to the static methodology document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.

questions.explanation: Caching the static methodology document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; B removes needed content; D is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production copilot, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and D accept the described dysfunction; C addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a recent forecast-quality regression was caused by a prompt change, a model-version change, or a CRM schema change — all three happened in the same release week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and C guess without evidence; D gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a forecast-narrative summary must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the sales-forecasting copilot is, to track over time.

choices.text: Use adoption rate alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, safety) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.
A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and D oversimplify to a single lossy number; B refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data-residency, retention, and access-logging design in the final weeks before the first plant's go-live, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: Cross-border data-residency and retention requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.
This sequencing carries no risk since compliance can always be added right before launch.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
A single global data-residency standard applies uniformly regardless of which country's plant is involved.

questions.explanation: Cross-border data-residency and retention requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. B and C understate real architectural impact; D wrongly assumes a single uniform standard applies across every jurisdiction.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: A regional team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the production-quality assistant produces, framing it as the safest governance posture ahead of the multi-country rollout.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for a multinational manufacturing deployment.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
This approach is required by ISO quality standards regardless of other considerations.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; C misattributes this requirement to a standard that doesn't actually mandate it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: The production-quality assistant must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from freeform operator notes, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed if they're observed in production first.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.
These risks are exclusive to consumer-facing use cases, not internal manufacturing tools.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; B assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; D is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Plant managers ask whether the assistant's quality-flagging decisions could produce disparate outcomes across different plants due to uneven historical sensor-data quality.

choices.text: This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Disparate impact across plants is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final shutdown decisions, not any assistive system.

Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects each plant's actual sensor and process conditions and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness across plants, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; B and C make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. questions.prompt: Across Ferrum's 200-person engineering organization, Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some teams have conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by site.

Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated global team to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption across a distributed organization.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the organization.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a safety-adjacent system.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a safety-adjacent system. A, B, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for this context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. questions.prompt: A production incident at one plant traces back to a Claude Code-generated sensor-threshold change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated logic or in how the plant's control system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigation.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.
Disable Claude Code for the entire engineering organization following any incident.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes across every plant regardless of relevance.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; C is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; B ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice; D over-engineers the one-off task.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)

choices.text: Access logging is optional if the system has role-based permissions.
Only failed access attempts need to be logged.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.
Audit logging can be added later without architectural impact.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and D each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires across jurisdictions.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders, since they'll relay information to the others.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences to save effort.
Skip stakeholder communication until the rollout is fully complete at every plant.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by plant-operations, legal, and engineering audiences alike. B, C, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders, and adjust the design and timeline accordingly.
Restart the entire multi-country rollout from scratch regardless of the change's actual scope.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. A and B mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration are entirely each plant's operations team's responsibility.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the rollout contract is signed.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code.
