Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.

Frame the architecture around transformation, since the actual driver is a new capability the current process entirely lacks, not a faster version of an existing one.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction, since underwriting automation always reduces cost.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar and let the build proceed without one.

questions.explanation: The actual driver is a capability the current process entirely lacks (a new specialty line), which is a transformation story, not an efficiency one. A and C misname the pillar discovery actually surfaced; D skips framing entirely.

An augmented LLM pattern, since a single retrieval-enhanced call can underwrite any commercial policy.
An agentic pattern, since the right sequence of steps varies by case and depends on intermediate findings uncovered during review.
Whichever pattern requires the fewest engineering resources, since the patterns are functionally interchangeable.

A assumes a predictability underwriting doesn't have here; B undersells the orchestration needed; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability and consistent error handling.
Merge all four responsibilities into one subagent to avoid coordination overhead.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industrial wants Claude to answer plant engineers' questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of maintenance manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and work-order history. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most engineer questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-sensor diagnostic reasoning, and a small fraction are simple lookups (e.g., a threshold value).

choices.text: Use one fixed model tier for all questions, regardless of complexity.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.
Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.

Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for the deep multi-sensor diagnostic cases.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex diagnostic questions. A and B ignore fit-to-task; C sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industrial wants Claude to answer plant engineers' questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of maintenance manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and work-order history. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (engineer persona, safety-disclaimer language, formatting rules) followed by retrieved document excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce both latency and cost across the high query volume.
Put retrieved content first since it's most relevant to the specific query.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industrial wants Claude to answer plant engineers' questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of maintenance manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and work-order history. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form maintenance manuals with short structured data (sensor telemetry logs and vibration thresholds).

choices.text: One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form manuals can serve both content types equally well.
Structured telemetry data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form manuals need different chunking than structured telemetry records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and C ignore this mismatch; B discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industrial wants Claude to answer plant engineers' questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of maintenance manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and work-order history. questions.prompt: Engineer queries range from exact lookups ("current vibration threshold for pump model X") to conceptual questions ("why has bearing failure on line 3 increased over the last quarter").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and C force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industrial wants Claude to answer plant engineers' questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of maintenance manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and work-order history. questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the client's real goal is to reduce dwell time at distribution hubs by 30% using existing staff and equipment — not new capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around efficiency, and build success metrics around dwell-time reduction per existing resource rather than novel capability.
Frame the architecture around transformation, since AI projects should aim to create new capability.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction exclusively, regardless of what discovery surfaced.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since the system either works or it doesn't.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (dwell-time reduction with existing staff/equipment) is an efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. B, C, and D either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (classification) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

Present the complete technical architecture diagram with no simplification.
Describe input → processing → output → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against defensibility and throughput goals, without requiring them to understand implementation internals.
Skip a high-level description and move directly into a live system demo.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; B is too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely.

Build full support for regulatory-investigation privilege rules now, guessing at undefined requirements.
Design the current decomposition and subagent boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase until next year's requirements are finalized.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A ignores a known future need entirely; B wastes effort guessing at undefined requirements; D blocks current delivery unnecessarily.

Rely on the original architect remaining available indefinitely instead of documenting.
Documentation is unnecessary if the code and prompts are well-organized.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. You are architecting model tiering, prompting, and the retrieval layer that connects the platform to a constantly growing corpus of publications and structured trial data.
questions.prompt: Most literature-review questions on Verdant's platform are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many trial reports, and a small fraction are simple lookups (e.g., a single drug's approval date).

choices.text: Use one fixed model tier for every question, regardless of complexity.

Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical synthesis questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for deep multi-document cases.
Always use the fastest, cheapest tier to control cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality regardless of question type.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and C ignore fit-to-task; D sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. You are architecting model tiering, prompting, and the retrieval layer that connects the platform to a constantly growing corpus of publications and structured trial data.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (regulatory-affairs persona, citation format, formatting rules) followed by retrieved excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order has no effect on cost or latency for this workload.
Interleave system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.
Put retrieved content first, since it's most specific to the query.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved excerpts after it, to reduce latency and cost across high query volume.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, B, and C all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form journal articles and trial reports with short structured records (a table of adverse-event counts by dose).

choices.text: Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't fit.
One chunking strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well.
Structured adverse-event data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size everywhere to avoid maintaining multiple strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. B and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. choices.text: Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Query pattern has no bearing on which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. B and C force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. You are architecting model tiering, prompting, and the retrieval layer that connects the platform to a constantly growing corpus of publications and structured trial data.
questions.prompt: Regulatory-affairs reviewers need citations that reliably map each claim to a specific source document and section, and prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite your sources" without further structure.
Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (document, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible source for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted documents at the end of the response.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. A, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. questions.prompt: Two retrieved sources report different adverse-event rates for the same trial arm — likely because one reports crude incidence and the other reports incidence adjusted for exposure time.

choices.text: Average the two figures and present the average as the answer.
Omit the adverse-event rate entirely since the sources disagree.
Always prefer whichever source was retrieved first.
Present both figures explicitly annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely methodological explanation, rather than silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and likely methodological explanation preserves the actual information for the reviewer rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard or obscure a genuine data conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: A prompt instructing the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.
Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Post-process every response to strip any text before the first `{`.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. B and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; D doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. Hard-code the safety-report integration into this platform's application code only.
Paste the entire safety-report corpus into every prompt.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. B, C, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full trial-registry catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Progressive discovery — querying a catalog resource as needed — scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the registry grows.
Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. B and C ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; D removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: A researcher asks a question requiring the model to reason step by step across several trial reports and journal articles before concluding whether a safety signal is emerging.

choices.text: Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective for this kind of question.
A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-document synthesis question.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple documents regardless of prompting approach.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. A, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, disclaimer language, formatting rules) across several different researcher-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Modular prompts are the same mechanism as prompt caching.
Standardization across features isn't achievable through prompt design.
Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; B conflates two distinct mechanisms; C denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. You are architecting model tiering, prompting, and the retrieval layer that connects the platform to a constantly growing corpus of publications and structured trial data.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific figure from the correctly retrieved source document.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted figures against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.
This is a pure model limitation with no architectural mitigation available.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C doesn't address correctness; D incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. You are architecting model tiering, prompting, and the retrieval layer that connects the platform to a constantly growing corpus of publications and structured trial data.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether researcher-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the platform.

choices.text: Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, rather than defaulting to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. B, C, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer benchmark scores always mean better production behavior.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and C assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; B over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Verdant Biosciences operates a literature-review platform that helps pharmacovigilance and regulatory-affairs teams synthesize findings across journal articles, clinical-trial registries, and internal safety reports. questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed, well-cited answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and D all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: TalentBridge's team currently measures only resume-screening throughput and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or fairness.

choices.text: Throughput alone is sufficient since it's the assistant's primary purpose.

Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness as first-class metrics — an assistant that screens quickly but is slow elsewhere, too expensive, or biased still fails overall.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Fairness metrics are only relevant if a complaint is filed.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it screens quickly. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for bias-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially bias-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)

Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since outreach-message changes are low-risk by nature.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; C confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue — inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content — which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; D avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled refresh of the job-requisition database, the assistant starts recommending mismatched candidates, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since the mismatches look erratic.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and D would not specifically correlate with a requisition-database refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average match-quality score.

A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since match quality is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence screening decisions by 80%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every role and candidate segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.
Segment accuracy by role and candidate source before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by role and candidate source before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; C over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new screening prompt improves throughput, but the team hasn't checked whether it also changed the false-negative rate for genuinely qualified candidates who should have advanced.

choices.text: Throughput alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.
Check the qualified-candidate false-negative rate specifically before shipping — an isolated throughput improvement could be masking an increase in inappropriately filtered strong candidates.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot (Questions 16–30)

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and D ignore or sacrifice fit-to-task; C forces one tier onto queries with very different needs.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. B, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.prompt: A dispatch recommendation assigns the wrong-skilled technician. Investigation shows the skill-matrix lookup was correct and retrieved properly, and the model's job-summary paraphrase mischaracterized the required skill.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the indexing pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled technician-roster and skill-matrix refresh, the assistant starts making poor assignments, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. B, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a roster/skill-matrix refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Utilities uses a Claude-powered assistant to triage and assign field technicians to service jobs based on urgency, required skills, and location. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average assignment-accuracy score.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-region or per-job-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence dispatch decisions by 75%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.
Segment accuracy by region and job type before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by region and job type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; C over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prioritization prompt improves on-time-arrival rate, but the team hasn't checked whether it increased mis-escalations of complex, safety-critical jobs that should route to senior technicians.

choices.text: On-time-arrival rate alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Check the escalation-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated on-time improvement could be masking an increase in inappropriate routing of complex, safety-critical jobs.
False-positive escalation behavior is not something evaluation can measure.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated on-time-arrival improvement could mask a worsened escalation failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Utilities uses a Claude-powered assistant to triage and assign field technicians to service jobs based on urgency, required skills, and location. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A subset of dispatch assignments are technically correct (right skill match) but rated poorly by technicians in satisfaction surveys, often citing unreasonable travel distance.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves satisfaction.
Investigate a dimension beyond skill-match correctness — e.g., travel burden or workload balance — since "accurate but poorly rated" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Ignore technician satisfaction scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (travel burden, workload balance) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Utilities uses a Claude-powered assistant to triage and assign field technicians to service jobs based on urgency, required skills, and location. questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends full technician-roster history plus a large static skill-matrix reference document on every dispatch decision.

choices.text: Apply prompt caching to the static skill-matrix document and consider trimming or summarizing older roster history to reduce redundant token cost.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.
Remove the skill-matrix document entirely to save tokens.
This has no optimization opportunity since full history is always required.

questions.explanation: Caching the static skill-matrix document and trimming/summarizing older roster history directly reduces redundant token cost. D denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production system, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a roster-data schema change — all three shipped in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a dispatch-summary output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the dispatch assistant is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.
Use on-time-arrival rate alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, safety) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Team Enablement for an Insurance Claims Modernization (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Harborline Insurance is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists claims adjusters with intake, coverage lookup, and payout recommendations, alongside a 25-person claims-engineering team using Claude Code internally to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data flow, retention, and access-logging design in the final week before launch, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: State insurance-regulation requirements around data residency, retention, and access control can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.
This sequencing carries no risk since compliance can always be added right before launch.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
HIPAA, not state insurance regulation, is the relevant regime for this claims system.

questions.explanation: State insurance-regulation requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. B and C understate real architectural impact; D misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Team Enablement for an Insurance Claims Modernization (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single claims-adjudication output, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for regulated AI systems.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
This approach is required by GDPR regardless of other considerations.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; C misattributes this to GDPR, which isn't the relevant regime described.

questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from claimant-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

These risks are exclusive to non-insurance use cases.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; B is factually wrong.

Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final payout decisions, not any assistive system.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a regulated system.

Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

Disable Claude Code for the team entirely following any incident.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes regardless of relevance.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; B over-engineers the one-off task; C ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders, and adjust the design and timeline accordingly.

This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration are entirely the operations team's responsibility.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ironclad Manufacturing wants Claude to help maintenance technicians diagnose equipment issues using both general reasoning and retrieval over equipment manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and historical maintenance records. questions.prompt: Most technician questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step diagnostic reasoning across sensor history and manuals, and a small fraction are simple lookups (e.g., part numbers).

choices.text: Use one fixed model tier for all questions, regardless of complexity.

Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for the deep diagnostic cases.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.
Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and C ignore fit-to-task; D sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce both latency and cost across the high query volume.
Put retrieved content first since it's most relevant to the specific query.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, B, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and D ignore this mismatch; B discards useful structured data.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (document, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. A, B, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

Present both figures explicitly annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely explanation (e.g., differing revision dates), rather than silently picking one.

questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific statistic from the correctly retrieved source publication.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted figures against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; C incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and B assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; D over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved document excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.
Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. B, C, and D all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: TalentBridge Staffing built a Claude-powered assistant that screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach, and answers recruiter questions about pipeline status. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only resume-screening throughput and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety/fairness.

choices.text: Throughput alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness as first-class metrics — a system that screens quickly but is biased, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Fairness metrics are only relevant if a complaint is filed.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it screens quickly. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario_context: TalentBridge Staffing built a Claude-powered assistant that screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach, and answers recruiter questions about pipeline status. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past resumes.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for fairness-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially fairness-relevant edge cases. A, C, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all traffic immediately and monitor for problems.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the indexing pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and C would not specifically correlate with a job-requisition data refresh.

questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency of resume screening but is worried about hurting accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Segment accuracy by role and candidate type before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by role/candidate type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

choices.text: Throughput alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
False-negative behavior on this dimension is not something evaluation can measure.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.
Check the fairness-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated throughput improvement could be masking a disparate increase in false negatives for a specific group.

questions.explanation: An isolated throughput improvement could mask a worsened fairness-related failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and C ship without adequate testing; B incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.

Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves recruiter satisfaction.
Ignore recruiter feedback scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (clarity, completeness, actionability) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; C assumes a fix without diagnosis.

Apply prompt caching to the static hiring-policy document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.
Remove the hiring-policy document entirely to save tokens.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.

questions.explanation: Caching the static hiring-policy document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; D is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. B and D accept the described dysfunction; C addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and C guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and C misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

Use screening throughput alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. B and C oversimplify to a single lossy number; D refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
HIPAA, not FedRAMP, is the relevant regime for a public-sector benefits system.
FedRAMP-driven data boundary, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.

questions.explanation: FedRAMP-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and B understate real architectural impact; C misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
This approach is required by FedRAMP regardless of other considerations.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; C misattributes this to FedRAMP, which doesn't mandate universal review.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; B assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; D is factually wrong.

This concern only applies to systems making final eligibility decisions, not any assistive system.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. B and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a FedRAMP-authorized system. B, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and C skip diagnosis; D is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.prompt: Most buyer questions to the copilot are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many SKUs and vendors, and a small fraction are simple lookups (for example, "current on-hand units for SKU 4471").

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. B and D sacrifice fit-to-task or quality; C ignores complexity variation entirely.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and B ignore this mismatch; D discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Mutual Insurance is modernizing its claims-intake and reserve-estimation systems with a Claude-powered assistant, and its 25-person claims engineering team uses Claude Code internally for day-to-day development. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment, and developer enablement for the program.
questions.prompt: The claims operations team asks whether the system's payout recommendations could produce disparate outcomes across different policyholder demographics.

choices.text: This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final payout decisions, not any assistive system.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Mutual Insurance is modernizing its claims-intake and reserve-estimation systems with a Claude-powered assistant, and its 25-person claims engineering team uses Claude Code internally for day-to-day development. choices.text: Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Have each engineer individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. B and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a regulated system.
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Team Enablement for an Insurance Claims Modernization (Questions 46–60)
