questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data flow, retention, and access-logging design in the final week before launch, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: This sequencing carries no risk since compliance can always be added right before launch.
HIPAA-driven data residency, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
FedRAMP, not HIPAA, is the relevant regime for a healthcare client.

questions.explanation: HIPAA-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and C understate real architectural impact; D misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the patient-intake system produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for healthcare AI systems.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.
This approach is required by GDPR regardless of other considerations.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this to GDPR, which isn't the relevant regime described.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from patient-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed if they're observed in production first.
These risks are exclusive to non-healthcare use cases.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The clinical operations team asks whether the system's decisions could produce disparate outcomes across different patient demographics.

choices.text: This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final clinical decisions, not any assistive system.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The 30-person clinical operations team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some staff have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Have each staff member individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. B and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes in this healthcare context to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a regulated system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a regulated system.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, B, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated data-handling change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigation.
Disable Claude Code for the team entirely following any incident.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes regardless of relevance.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and C skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The clinical operations team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly compliance summary report) versus a one-off exploratory coding task.

choices.text: Build both as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time they're needed.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed what patient-related data through the system and when.

choices.text: Access logging is optional if the system has role-based permissions.
Audit logging can be added later without architectural impact.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.
Only failed access attempts need to be logged.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and D each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The steering committee for this deployment includes clinical, legal, and engineering stakeholders with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders, since they'll relay information to the others.
Skip stakeholder communication until the system is fully built.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences to save effort.
Tailor architectural communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms clinical and legal stakeholders can evaluate against their own priorities, not just engineering metrics.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by clinical, legal, and engineering audiences alike. A, C, and B each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: Midway through the project, the clinical team's requirements shift meaningfully based on a new regulatory guidance document.

choices.text: Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders, and adjust the design and timeline accordingly.
Refuse to incorporate the change since requirements were already agreed upon.
Incorporate the change silently without informing stakeholders of the impact.
Restart the entire project from scratch regardless of the change's actual scope.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. B and C mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: After launch, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending at handoff to the operations team.

choices.text: This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration are entirely the operations team's responsibility.
Lifecycle management includes monitoring and iteration based on production signal as part of the architect's ongoing responsibility, not just discovery through handoff.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the contract is signed.
Monitoring is only necessary if a major incident occurs.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through handoff. A, C, and D all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: Documentation for this system currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: This level of documentation is sufficient since the "what" is all a future team needs.
Documenting reasoning is unnecessary overhead in a regulated environment.
Documentation should also capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — so a future team can safely extend or modify the system without re-deriving that context.
Only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system, making documentation moot.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system, especially in a regulated context. A, B, and D all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The clinical operations team wants Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting documentation, exploring an unfamiliar module) but is unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves time on every task category by default.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks without evaluation.
Mandate Claude Code usage for all tasks regardless of measured benefit.

Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction (e.g., repetitive documentation drafting, codebase exploration) versus cases where review overhead may exceed time saved, rather than assuming a blanket benefit.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; B forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance, Compliance, and Team Enablement for a Healthcare Deployment
questions.scenario_context: A healthcare client is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes patient intake information and assists a 30-person clinical operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, regulatory compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: A recurring operational issue is that different engineers debug similar Claude Code integration failures independently, each re-deriving the same integration-layer-versus-model-output triage process.

choices.text: This is an acceptable ongoing inefficiency with no architectural fix.

Document the triage process (how to distinguish integration-layer failures from model-output failures for this system) as shared operational knowledge, reducing redundant re-derivation across the team.
Restrict debugging to a single designated engineer.
The issue can only be resolved by switching to a different tool entirely.

questions.explanation: Documenting the shared triage process turns individually re-derived knowledge into reusable operational knowledge, directly addressing the redundant-effort problem described. B accepts avoidable inefficiency; C and D propose disproportionate structural changes instead of the straightforward documentation fix. --- *End of Practice Exam 1.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery with Meridian's operations leadership reveals the actual goal is booking 2.5x more freight volume through the existing carrier network with the same dispatch staff, at the same average booking cycle time — not new routing capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since AI initiatives should always aim to introduce new capability.
Frame the architecture around efficiency, and build success metrics around bookings processed per dispatcher rather than novel capability.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction exclusively, regardless of what discovery surfaced.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since a working system speaks for itself.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (more volume, same headcount, same cycle time) is a throughput/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A, C, and D either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Generating the standard customs export declaration for an international shipment follows the same five-step sequence every time — regardless of shipment type, carrier, or destination country.

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since customs processes always warrant autonomous step selection.
An augmented LLM pattern, since a single retrieval-enhanced call is sufficient for any customs task.
Whichever pattern minimizes initial build time, since the two patterns are functionally interchangeable.
A fixed workflow, since the steps are predetermined and identical for every shipment regardless of case specifics.

questions.explanation: A predetermined sequence identical for every case, regardless of shipment specifics, is the defining case for a fixed workflow. A overstates the need for autonomous step selection; B undersells the multi-step nature of the task; C treats two non-interchangeable patterns as equivalent.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (carrier-rate lookup, customs-compliance check, exception triage, shipment-status synthesis).

choices.text: Let each subagent pass its results directly to whichever subagent needs them next, to minimize hops through the coordinator.
Merge all four responsibilities into a single subagent to eliminate coordination overhead.
Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
Let subagents communicate directly with each other, but log the traffic afterward for review.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. A and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; B discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why the customs-compliance subagent runs on a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the shipment-status-synthesis subagent.

choices.text: "The higher tier is used because compliance work is more important" is a sufficient answer on its own.
Avoid explaining the tier difference in detail, since stakeholders don't need to understand model internals.

Explain the tradeoff explicitly: customs-compliance analysis needs deeper reasoning that justifies the added cost/latency, while status synthesis is simpler and better served by a faster, cheaper tier.
Use the same tier across every subagent for consistency, regardless of task difficulty.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. A and B withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The design must align the technical architecture to a specific business value pillar Meridian's leadership actually cares about, distinct from a generic "we added AI" narrative.

choices.text: Efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and service-level performance are examples of such pillars; the chosen one should drive both the architecture and its success metrics.
Any AI-powered logistics system inherently demonstrates transformation, so no further framing is required.
Business value pillars are a sales and marketing concern, not an architectural one.
The pillar should be selected after launch, based on whichever benefit turns out easiest to measure.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery interviews with dock and dispatch staff repeatedly surface fear that automated carrier selection and exception handling will eliminate their roles.

choices.text: Treat this sentiment as a real implicit constraint alongside the explicit technical requirements — it will shape adoption, rollout sequencing, and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter most.
Ignore the sentiment since it is not a stated technical requirement.
Proceed with the technical design and let change management address the sentiment separately, with no architectural input.
Recommend against the project entirely based on the sentiment alone.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. B and C treat it as out of scope; D overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the technical case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Every subagent performs its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition routes only standard ocean-freight shipments into the pipeline — hazmat and oversized-cargo shipments are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through untouched.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent specifically to catch miscellaneous edge cases.
Add a prompt instruction telling the existing subagents to flag shipment types they don't recognize.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so they can handle any shipment type themselves.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers all shipment categories, including hazmat and oversized cargo, rather than tuning the existing subagents.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole shipment categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. A, B, and C all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The architecture currently produces a final exception-resolution recommendation with no mechanism to learn from dispatcher overrides or downstream outcomes over time.

choices.text: Add a feedback loop capturing dispatcher overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component, so the system can improve after deployment.
This is acceptable, since the initial design already reflects current best practice.
Feedback loops are a data-science concern unrelated to the architecture.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, with no hooks in the current design.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures dispatcher overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment. B, C, and D all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Meridian wants a single enhanced LLM call — with tool access to the live shipment-tracking API — to answer straightforward "where is my shipment" questions, without any multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: This calls for a full multi-agent architecture regardless of how simple the underlying task is.
An augmented LLM pattern (a single call enhanced with tool access) fits this simpler augmentation need without the overhead of agentic orchestration.
This requires a fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps.
This cannot be built with Claude, since it does not involve autonomous agent behavior.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with tool access, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and C over-engineer a simple augmentation need; D is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The carrier-rate-lookup subagent's toolset has grown to include tools for tasks like invoice generation and driver scheduling that are unrelated to rate lookup.

choices.text: This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; the unrelated tools should be removed or relocated to a more appropriate subagent.
This has no architectural downside as long as the subagent's prompt is well-written.
More tools always improve a subagent's flexibility and should be encouraged.
The fix is to increase the subagent's context window.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not just writing around it. B and C ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently processes each shipment sequentially through carrier-rate lookup, customs-compliance check, exception triage, and status synthesis — even though customs-compliance check and exception triage have no dependency on each other's output.

choices.text: Sequential processing is required for auditability in a logistics context.
Combine customs-compliance check and exception triage into a single subagent to avoid the sequencing question.
Parallelization is not possible within a coordinator/subagent architecture.
Run customs-compliance check and exception triage as independent, parallel subagent calls once carrier-rate lookup completes, rather than sequentially.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (carrier-rate lookup) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. A and C misstate real constraints; B avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Meridian's steering committee, unfamiliar with the technical details, asks how the end-to-end architecture should be described at a high level.

choices.text: Present only the model names and per-call token costs involved.
Describe input → processing → output → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against business outcomes, without requiring them to understand implementation internals.
Present the full technical architecture diagram with no simplification.
Skip a high-level description and move directly into an implementation demo.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; C is too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A competing vendor proposes a single generalist agent with every tool (rate lookup, compliance, exception handling, tracking) rather than a coordinator with specialized subagents.

choices.text: A single agent holding every tool and responsibility is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents scoped to narrower roles.
A single generalist agent scales better as the tool count grows.
There is no meaningful architectural difference between the two approaches.
Specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice with no reliability benefit.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. B, C, and D understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with dispatch and operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The architecture must eventually support a new shipment category (cross-border rail freight) Meridian plans to launch next year, but detailed requirements aren't available yet.

choices.text: Build full support for cross-border rail freight now, guessing at the requirements.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase until the future requirements are finalized.
Ignore the future category entirely until requirements exist.
Design the current decomposition and tool/subagent boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A wastes effort guessing at undefined requirements; B blocks current delivery unnecessarily; C ignores a known future need entirely.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks, a global logistics operator, wants to modernize freight booking, carrier selection, exception handling (delays, customs holds, damaged cargo), and shipment tracking. choices.text: Document only the final configuration values, since implementation is self-explanatory.
Rely on the original architect remaining available indefinitely instead of documenting.
Documentation is unnecessary if the code is well organized.
Document the architecture and the reasoning ("why") behind key decisions — pattern choices, decomposition boundaries, tier selections — not just the final "what."

questions.explanation: Documenting the reasoning behind key decisions, not just final values, is what lets a future team safely extend the system without the original architect present. A, B, and C all leave the actual knowledge transfer gap unaddressed.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most attorney questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many opinions, and a small fraction are simple citation lookups.

choices.text: Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.

Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple citation lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for deep multi-step research.
Use one fixed model tier for all questions, regardless of complexity.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and B ignore fit-to-task; D sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (attorney persona, citation-format rules, jurisdiction-handling instructions) followed by retrieved opinion excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce both latency and cost across high query volume.
Put retrieved content first since it's most relevant to the specific query.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form court opinions with short structured data (a table of statute citations and effective dates).

choices.text: Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form opinions need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form opinions can serve both content types equally well.
Structured statute data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. B and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorney queries range from exact lookups ("cite for Smith v. Jones, 2019") to conceptual questions ("how has the standard for qualified immunity evolved across circuits").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact citation lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and D force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; B denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorneys need citations that reliably map each claim to a specific opinion and pincite, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without further structure.
Add pincites after the fact by searching for a plausible source for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted opinions at the end of each response.
Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (case, pincite, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. A, B, and C all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved opinions from different circuits state the applicable standard differently — likely reflecting a genuine circuit split rather than an error.

choices.text: Average the two standards and present a blended formulation.
Omit the standard entirely since the sources disagree.
Always prefer whichever opinion was retrieved first.
Present both standards explicitly, annotated as a circuit split, with source attribution, rather than silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and the likely explanation (a circuit split) preserves the actual information for the attorney rather than resolving a real disagreement arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard or obscure a genuine conflict in the sources.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.
Post-process every response to strip leading text before the first `{`.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; B doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: CaseLantern needs to connect to a proprietary internal memoranda system, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

choices.text: Hard-code the memoranda integration into this platform's application code only.
Build an MCP server exposing the memoranda operations as tools/resources, reusable across the multiple internal Claude-powered tools that need it.
Paste the entire memoranda corpus into every prompt.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, C, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full case-law catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
There is no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.
Progressive discovery (querying a catalog resource as needed) scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the corpus grows.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: An attorney asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved opinions before concluding.

choices.text: A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-opinion synthesis question.
Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple opinions regardless of prompting approach.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-opinion synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: CaseLantern wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, jurisdiction disclaimers, formatting rules) across several different attorney-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Modular prompts are the same thing as prompt caching.
Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).
Standardization across features isn't achievable through prompt design.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; B conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific holding from the correctly retrieved opinion.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted holdings against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted holdings against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C doesn't address correctness; D incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether attorney-facing latency SLAs should factor into model-tier selection for the research platform.

choices.text: Yes — model-tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.
Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. B, C, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and C assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; D over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: CaseLantern, a legal research platform serving litigation attorneys, wants Claude to answer case-law research questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of court opinions, statutes, and internal firm memoranda. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved opinion excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long opinions, never for typical queries.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only forecast-adoption rate (how often reps accept the copilot's forecast) and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Adoption rate alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — a system that gets adopted but is too slow, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if adoption looks healthy. A, B, and C each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past forecasting scenarios.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves forecast quality before rolling it out to all revenue teams.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all teams immediately and monitor for problems.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Change the prompt and the underlying model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; C confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: A forecast is materially wrong. Investigation shows the underlying pipeline data (historical deal velocity, quota attainment) was correctly retrieved, and the model's narrative summary misinterpreted the trend direction.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the data pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (misinterpreting correctly retrieved data), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than pipeline changes.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.

questions.explanation: Correct pipeline retrieval plus a misinterpreted trend direction is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than pipeline or model-tier changes. A and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled CRM data-sync refresh, the copilot starts producing confident but incorrect quarterly forecasts, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Investigate the data pipeline/CRM-sync layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data-refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at the data pipeline/CRM-sync layer. B, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a scheduled data refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting forecast accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average forecast-accuracy score.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-segment or per-product-line breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and C accept a monitoring blind spot; D drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence forecasts by 75%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by product line and deal size before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by product line and deal size before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves forecast-adoption rate, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate at which the copilot overconfidently forecasts deals that later slip.

choices.text: Check the deal-slippage-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated adoption-rate improvement could be masking an increase in overconfident forecasts on deals that later fall through.
Adoption rate alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.
Deal-slippage failure behavior is not something evaluation can measure.

questions.explanation: An isolated adoption-rate improvement could mask a worsened deal-slippage failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. B and C ship without adequate testing; D incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of forecasts are numerically accurate but rated poorly by reps in feedback surveys.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves rep satisfaction.

Investigate a dimension beyond numerical accuracy — e.g., explanation clarity, actionability of the narrative, or tone — since "accurate but poorly rated" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Ignore rep satisfaction scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (explanation clarity, actionability, tone) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends full quarter-to-date deal history plus a large static forecasting-methodology document on every turn of a multi-turn coaching conversation.

choices.text: This has no optimization opportunity since full history is always required.
Remove the methodology document entirely to save tokens.
Apply prompt caching to the static methodology document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.

questions.explanation: Caching the static methodology document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; B removes needed content; D is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production copilot, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and D accept the described dysfunction; C addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a recent forecast-quality regression was caused by a prompt change, a model-version change, or a CRM schema change — all three happened in the same release week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and C guess without evidence; D gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a forecast-narrative summary must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Quotient Analytics, a B2B software company, has had a Claude-powered sales-forecasting copilot in production for revenue teams for eight months. You are responsible for the evaluation strategy, A/B testing prompt and model changes, and diagnosing quality regressions.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the sales-forecasting copilot is, to track over time.

choices.text: Use adoption rate alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, safety) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.
A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and D oversimplify to a single lossy number; B refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.
