questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data-residency, retention, and access-logging design in the final weeks before the first plant's go-live, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: Cross-border data-residency and retention requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.
This sequencing carries no risk since compliance can always be added right before launch.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
A single global data-residency standard applies uniformly regardless of which country's plant is involved.

questions.explanation: Cross-border data-residency and retention requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. B and C understate real architectural impact; D wrongly assumes a single uniform standard applies across every jurisdiction.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: A regional team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the production-quality assistant produces, framing it as the safest governance posture ahead of the multi-country rollout.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for a multinational manufacturing deployment.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
This approach is required by ISO quality standards regardless of other considerations.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; C misattributes this requirement to a standard that doesn't actually mandate it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: The production-quality assistant must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from freeform operator notes, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed if they're observed in production first.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.
These risks are exclusive to consumer-facing use cases, not internal manufacturing tools.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; B assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; D is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Plant managers ask whether the assistant's quality-flagging decisions could produce disparate outcomes across different plants due to uneven historical sensor-data quality.

choices.text: This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Disparate impact across plants is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final shutdown decisions, not any assistive system.

Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects each plant's actual sensor and process conditions and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness across plants, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; B and C make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Across Ferrum's 200-person engineering organization, Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some teams have conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by site.

choices.text: Have each engineer individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated global team to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption across a distributed organization.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the organization.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Ferrum wants Claude Code-generated code changes to production-quality-assistant components to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a manufacturing safety-adjacent system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a safety-adjacent system.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a safety-adjacent system. A, B, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for this context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: A production incident at one plant traces back to a Claude Code-generated sensor-threshold change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated logic or in how the plant's control system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigation.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.
Disable Claude Code for the entire engineering organization following any incident.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes across every plant regardless of relevance.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; C is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: A regional engineering team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly cross-plant quality-variance report) versus a one-off exploratory investigation of an unfamiliar legacy module.

choices.text: Build both as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time they're needed.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; B ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice; D over-engineers the one-off task.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Ferrum's compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed which plant's production data through the assistant, and when, across all twelve countries.

choices.text: Access logging is optional if the system has role-based permissions.
Only failed access attempts need to be logged.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.
Audit logging can be added later without architectural impact.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and D each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires across jurisdictions.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: The steering committee for the rollout includes plant-operations, legal/compliance, and engineering stakeholders across different countries, with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Tailor architectural communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms plant-operations and legal/compliance stakeholders can evaluate against their own priorities, not just engineering metrics.
Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders, since they'll relay information to the others.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences to save effort.
Skip stakeholder communication until the rollout is fully complete at every plant.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by plant-operations, legal, and engineering audiences alike. B, C, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Midway through the rollout, requirements shift meaningfully after a new cross-border data-transfer regulation is issued affecting several plants.

choices.text: Refuse to incorporate the change since requirements were already agreed upon.
Incorporate the change silently without informing stakeholders of the impact.

Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders, and adjust the design and timeline accordingly.
Restart the entire multi-country rollout from scratch regardless of the change's actual scope.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. A and B mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: After the first plant's go-live, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending at handoff to each plant's local operations team.

choices.text: Lifecycle management includes monitoring and iteration based on production signal as part of the architect's ongoing responsibility, not just discovery through handoff.
This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration are entirely each plant's operations team's responsibility.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the rollout contract is signed.
Monitoring is only necessary if a major incident occurs at a given plant.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through discovery and handoff. B, C, and D all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Documentation for the rollout currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, per-plant thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: This level of documentation is sufficient since the "what" is all a future team needs.
Documenting reasoning is unnecessary overhead in a multi-country regulated environment.
Only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system, making documentation moot.

Documentation should also capture the "why" behind key decisions — regulatory drivers, tradeoff reasoning per jurisdiction — so a future team can safely extend or modify the system without re-deriving that context.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (regulatory drivers, tradeoff reasoning per jurisdiction) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system across a multi-country deployment. A, B, and C all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: Engineering leads across several plants want Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting maintenance documentation, exploring an unfamiliar legacy module) but are unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves time on every task category by default.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks without evaluation.
Mandate Claude Code usage for all tasks regardless of measured benefit.

Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction (e.g., repetitive documentation drafting, codebase exploration) versus cases where review overhead may exceed time saved, rather than assuming a blanket benefit.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; B forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Ferrum Industrial Group, a multinational manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-quality assistant across plants in twelve countries and enabling a 200-person global engineering organization to use Claude Code. You are responsible for governance, regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, and lifecycle management for the rollout.
questions.prompt: A recurring operational issue is that engineers at different plants debug similar Claude Code integration failures independently, each re-deriving the same integration-layer-versus-model-output triage process.

choices.text: This is an acceptable ongoing inefficiency with no architectural fix.
Document the triage process (how to distinguish integration-layer failures from model-output failures for this system) as shared operational knowledge, reducing redundant re-derivation across plants.
Restrict debugging to a single designated engineer across all plants.
The issue can only be resolved by switching to a different tool entirely.

questions.explanation: Documenting the shared triage process turns individually re-derived knowledge into reusable operational knowledge, directly addressing the redundant-effort problem described. A accepts avoidable inefficiency; C and D propose disproportionate structural changes instead of the straightforward documentation fix. --- *End of Practice Exam 2.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the firm's actual goal is reducing the per-matter cost of first-pass document review by using fewer contract attorneys, while maintaining the same review turnaround time — not adding entirely new review capabilities.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since AI-assisted review is inherently transformative.
Frame the architecture around performance SLAs exclusively, ignoring the cost objective discovery surfaced.
Frame the architecture around new capability, since first-pass review didn't previously use AI at all.
Frame the architecture around cost/efficiency, and build success metrics around cost-per-document and reviewer headcount rather than novel capability.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (fewer contract attorneys, same turnaround) is a cost/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A and C misname the pillar as transformation/new capability, and B drops the cost objective discovery actually surfaced.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Document intake, responsiveness classification, privilege review, and redaction each require different steps depending on document type, matter-specific protective order terms, and findings from prior steps (e.g., a privilege hit changes downstream handling).

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since the right steps vary by document and depend on intermediate findings.
A fixed workflow, since document review is a standardized business process.
An augmented LLM pattern, since a single enhanced call is sufficient for any matter.
Whichever pattern ships fastest, since the patterns are functionally interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by document type, protective-order terms, and intermediate findings (a privilege hit changing downstream handling) are the defining case for an agentic pattern. B assumes a predictability the scenario lacks; C undersells the orchestration needed; D ignores real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: In the proposed coordinator/subagent design, the privilege-review subagent identifies a document as privileged and needs the redaction subagent to apply redactions before production.

choices.text: Route the privilege determination through the coordinator, which then dispatches to the redaction subagent — preserving observability and consistent handling of privilege calls across the matter.
Let the privilege-review subagent call the redaction subagent directly to save a hop.
Merge privilege review and redaction into a single subagent to avoid coordination entirely.
Have every subagent broadcast its findings to all other subagents indiscriminately.

questions.explanation: Routing the privilege determination through the coordinator preserves observability and consistent handling of privilege calls across the matter. B and D sacrifice this for a shortcut or noise; C discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the responsiveness-classification and privilege-review subagents each independently re-run OCR on the same intake documents, since neither receives the intake subagent's OCR output.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent dedicated solely to OCR deduplication.
Give the intake subagent tool access to write directly into each downstream subagent's private context.
Fix the coordinator's data flow so intake's OCR output is passed downstream to each subagent that needs it, rather than having subagents redundantly regenerate it.
Increase the context window of the responsiveness-classification subagent so it can OCR faster.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while redundantly re-deriving the same OCR output is a coordinator data-flow problem, not a subagent capability gap. A, B, and D all patch around the issue instead of fixing the missing hand-off.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery with partners surfaces that what actually worries them is defensibility of privilege calls in front of a judge, not raw review speed or cost.

choices.text: Ignore this since cost was the pillar named in the original engagement letter.
Treat defensibility as identical to cost efficiency, since both are business concerns.
Reframe the pillar toward auditability/defensibility — accuracy, explainability, and audit trails for privilege calls — since that is what discovery actually surfaced, and design metrics around it.
Add defensibility as a documentation footnote without changing metrics or design.

questions.explanation: Discovery surfacing defensibility as the actual driving concern means the pillar and its metrics should shift toward auditability/explainability, not stay anchored to the originally named pillar. A and D ignore what discovery revealed; B conflates two distinct concerns.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery interviews reveal review attorneys are worried the AI will be used as the sole justification for withholding documents without attorney sign-off, exposing the firm to sanctions risk.

choices.text: Ignore the sentiment since it's a change-management issue, not architecture.
Proceed with full automation of withholding decisions and address the sentiment only through a communications campaign.
Treat this as a real constraint requiring a human-in-the-loop checkpoint before any document is withheld from production, and design the escalation path as part of the architecture.
Recommend the firm abandon the AI review project based on the sentiment alone.

questions.explanation: Adoption/liability sentiment about unsupervised withholding decisions is a real implicit constraint that should shape a specific HITL checkpoint in the architecture. A and B treat it as out of scope; D overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing the technical case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A partner asks why the privilege-review subagent uses a higher-capability model tier than the intake/OCR subagent.

choices.text: Explain the tradeoff: privilege determination requires nuanced legal reasoning that justifies the added cost/latency, while OCR/intake is comparatively mechanical and suited to a faster, cheaper tier.
Say the higher tier is used everywhere "to be safe," regardless of task.
Avoid explaining the difference, since partners don't need technical detail.
Say the tier choice was arbitrary and could be swapped without effect.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper legal reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. B and D remove or hide a deliberate, justified difference; C withholds reasoning partners need.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The current design produces final privilege/responsiveness calls with no mechanism to capture reviewing-attorney overrides for future improvement.

choices.text: This is acceptable; the initial classifier already reflects current best practice.
Feedback loops are a data-science concern unrelated to the architecture.
Defer any feedback mechanism to an undefined future phase with no design hooks today.
Add a feedback loop capturing attorney overrides and their reasons as a first-class architectural component, so the system can improve after deployment.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures attorney overrides and reasoning as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve post-deployment. A, B, and C all treat this component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A partner wants a single enhanced call — with retrieval over a matter's document set — to answer a quick question like "do we have any emails between X and Y," without multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: An augmented LLM pattern (a single call enhanced with retrieval) fits this simple augmentation need without the overhead of agentic orchestration.
This requires the full multi-agent e-discovery pipeline regardless of the simplicity of the ask.
This cannot be done with Claude, since it isn't a full agent.
This requires a fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. B and D over-engineer a simple augmentation need; C is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The intake/OCR subagent's toolset has grown to include billing-code lookup and calendar-scheduling tools unrelated to document intake.

choices.text: This has no downside as long as the prompt is well-written.
This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; unrelated tools should be removed or relocated to a more appropriate subagent.
More tools always increase flexibility and should be encouraged.
The fix is to enlarge the subagent's context window.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows; the fix is removing or relocating them. A and C ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design and for running discovery with litigation-support staff and partner stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently runs responsiveness classification and privilege review sequentially for each document, though neither depends on the other's output once intake/OCR completes.

choices.text: Run responsiveness classification and privilege review as independent, parallel subagent calls once intake completes, rather than sequentially.
Sequential processing is required for defensibility in litigation.
Parallelization isn't possible in a coordinator/subagent architecture.
Combine both into a single subagent to avoid the sequencing question.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (intake) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. questions.prompt: The firm's managing partners, unfamiliar with technical detail, ask how the e-discovery architecture should be described to the executive committee.

choices.text: Present only model names and token costs.
Present the full technical architecture diagram with no simplification.
Skip a high-level description and go straight to a live demo.

Describe intake → classification → privilege review → production → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against cost, risk, and turnaround outcomes, without requiring implementation detail.

questions.explanation: A steering-level audience needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A and B are the wrong level of detail; C skips the communication need entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm

questions.prompt: A competing vendor proposes one generalist agent holding every tool (OCR, classification, privilege review, redaction, production formatting) instead of a coordinator with specialized subagents.

choices.text: A single agent holding every tool and responsibility is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents scoped to narrower roles.
A single generalist agent scales better as tool count grows.
Specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice with no reliability benefit.
There's no meaningful architectural difference between the two approaches.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. B, C, and D understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.

questions.scenario_context: Harlow & Voss LLP, a 400-attorney litigation firm, is building a multi-agent e-discovery platform to review, classify, and produce documents for active matters. The platform must handle document intake/OCR, responsiveness classification, privilege review, redaction, and production formatting across matters governed by different protective orders. questions.prompt: The platform must eventually support foreign-language document review, a matter type planned for next year, but detailed requirements aren't finalized.

choices.text: Build full foreign-language support now, guessing at unspecified requirements.
Ignore future foreign-language needs until requirements are formally scoped.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase until future requirements are finalized.
Design the current decomposition and subagent/tool boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A wastes effort guessing at undefined requirements; B ignores a known future need entirely; C blocks current delivery unnecessarily.

Rely on the original architect remaining available indefinitely instead of documenting.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most scientist questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many studies, and a small fraction are simple lookups (e.g., "what was the primary endpoint in Study 204").

choices.text: Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.
Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.
Route by task difficulty — a fast tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for deep multi-step cases.
Use one fixed model tier for all questions regardless of complexity.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and D ignore fit-to-task; B sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (scientific-writing persona, citation format, disclaimer language) followed by retrieved excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.
Put retrieved content first, since it's most relevant to the specific query.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce latency and cost across high query volume.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, B, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form clinical study reports with short structured data (a table of adverse-event rates by treatment arm).

choices.text: One chunking/indexing strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.
Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form reports need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
Structured adverse-event data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and B ignore this mismatch; D discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: Scientist queries range from exact lookups ("primary endpoint for Study 204") to conceptual questions ("how has the safety narrative for Compound X evolved across trials").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and B force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: Scientists need citations that reliably map each claim to a specific study and section, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (study, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.
Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without further structure.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible source for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted documents at the end of each response.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved sources disagree on a trial's reported adverse-event rate by a small margin — likely different analysis populations (intent-to-treat vs. per-protocol).

choices.text: Present both figures explicitly annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely methodological explanation (e.g., ITT vs. per-protocol), rather than silently picking one.
Average the two figures and present the average.
Omit the adverse-event rate entirely, since sources disagree.
Always prefer whichever source was retrieved first.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and the likely methodological explanation preserves the actual information for the scientist rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. B, C, and D all discard or obscure a genuine data conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.
Post-process every response to strip leading text before the first `{`.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; D doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal study-repository system, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond this literature-review platform.

choices.text: Build an MCP server exposing the study-repository operations as tools/resources, reusable across the multiple internal Claude-powered tools that need it.
Hard-code the integration into this platform's application code only.
Paste the entire study repository into every prompt.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. B, C, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full study catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
Progressive discovery (querying a catalog resource as needed) scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the corpus grows.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and C ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; D removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: A scientist asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved studies before concluding.

choices.text: Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple documents regardless of prompting approach.
A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-study synthesis question.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-study synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. A, B, and C all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, disclaimer language, formatting rules) across several different scientist-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).
Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Modular prompts are the same thing as prompt caching.
Standardization across features isn't achievable with prompt design.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. B reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific figure from the correctly retrieved source document.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted figures against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; B incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether scientist-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Tiering for a Pharmaceutical Literature-Review Platform
questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; C over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario_context: Aventra Biosciences' medical affairs team needs Claude to answer scientist questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of clinical trial protocols, published literature, and internal study reports. You are architecting model selection, prompting, and the integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved study excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. B, C, and D all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only resume-screening throughput and hasn't defined targets for accuracy, latency, cost, or fairness.

choices.text: Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness as first-class metrics — a system that screens quickly but is inaccurate, slow to correct itself, expensive, or unfair still fails overall.
Throughput alone is sufficient, since it's the system's primary purpose.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Fairness metrics are only relevant if a complaint has already been filed.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it screens quickly. B, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past resumes.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for fairness-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially fairness-relevant edge cases. A, C, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new screening-prompt version improves accuracy before rolling it out to all requisitions.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all requisitions immediately and monitor for problems.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing, since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A candidate is incorrectly screened out. Investigation shows the underlying resume was parsed and retrieved correctly, and the model's screening rationale misread a clearly-stated qualification.

choices.text: This is a retrieval/parsing problem; fix the ingestion pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This is best characterized as a generation/reasoning issue (misreading correctly retrieved content), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than ingestion changes.

questions.explanation: Correct parsing plus a misread qualification is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than ingestion or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled update to the job-requisition template library, the assistant starts screening out qualified candidates at a higher rate, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Investigate the requisition-template/retrieval layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the template update event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since screening behavior changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a template-update event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at the requisition-template/retrieval layer. A, C, and D would not specifically correlate with that update.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency in outreach-message drafting but is worried about hurting quality, with no current data on where the configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and quality should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.

Optimize cost/latency/quality jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the quality bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing quality at unsustainable cost.
Quality should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "quality at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the quality bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts candidate outreach messages, and answers candidate FAQs for a mid-size tech company's talent acquisition team. It has been in production for six months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average screening-accuracy score.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-role or per-requisition-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.
