questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: TalentBridge's team currently measures only resume-screening throughput and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or fairness.

choices.text: Throughput alone is sufficient since it's the assistant's primary purpose.

Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness as first-class metrics — an assistant that screens quickly but is slow elsewhere, too expensive, or biased still fails overall.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Fairness metrics are only relevant if a complaint is filed.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/fairness should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it screens quickly. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past candidate resumes.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for bias-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially bias-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new outreach-message prompt improves candidate response rate before rolling it out to all traffic.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all traffic immediately and monitor for problems.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since outreach-message changes are low-risk by nature.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; C confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: A candidate's screening summary misstates their years of relevant experience. Investigation shows the resume was parsed and retrieved correctly, and the model's response paraphrased the experience section inaccurately.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the resume-parsing pipeline.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue — inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content — which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; D avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled refresh of the job-requisition database, the assistant starts recommending mismatched candidates, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since the mismatches look erratic.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and D would not specifically correlate with a requisition-database refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency in the screening pipeline but is worried about hurting candidate-match accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average match-quality score.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-role or per-source breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since match quality is captured by the eval suite alone.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence screening decisions by 80%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every role and candidate segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.
Segment accuracy by role and candidate source before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by role and candidate source before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; C over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new screening prompt improves throughput, but the team hasn't checked whether it also changed the false-negative rate for genuinely qualified candidates who should have advanced.

choices.text: Throughput alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.
Check the qualified-candidate false-negative rate specifically before shipping — an isolated throughput improvement could be masking an increase in inappropriately filtered strong candidates.
False-negative behavior on qualified candidates is not something evaluation can measure.

questions.explanation: An isolated throughput improvement could mask a worsened false-negative rate on qualified candidates; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and B ship without adequate testing; D incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of screening summaries are factually accurate but rated poorly by hiring managers.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Investigate a dimension beyond factual accuracy — e.g., tone, completeness, or actionability — since "accurate but poorly rated" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves hiring-manager satisfaction.
Ignore hiring-manager ratings in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (tone, completeness, actionability) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; C assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full conversation history plus a large static compliance-policy document on every turn of multi-turn candidate conversations.

choices.text: Apply prompt caching to the static compliance-policy document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.
Remove the compliance-policy document entirely to save tokens.
This has no optimization opportunity since full history is always required.

questions.explanation: Caching the static compliance-policy document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. D denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production system, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and D accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a recent quality regression was caused by a prompt change, a model version change, or a job-requisition data change — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and C guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that an outreach-message draft must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on drafts a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. B and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of an HR Recruiting Assistant
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered recruiting assistant screens resumes, drafts outreach messages, and answers candidate questions for TalentBridge, a mid-market staffing firm. It has been in production for four months, and you are responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality regressions, and optimizing the cost/latency/accuracy tradeoff as volume grows.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the recruiting assistant is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.
Use throughput alone as the single number, since it's the assistant's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, fairness) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: DCRM's architecture team is finalizing data-boundary, retention, and access-logging design in the final weeks before the ATO assessment, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: This sequencing carries no risk since compliance controls can always be added right before an ATO review.
Compliance only affects documentation submitted for the ATO package, not system architecture.
HIPAA, not FedRAMP, is the relevant regime for a state benefits agency.
FedRAMP-driven data-boundary, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.

questions.explanation: FedRAMP-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and B understate real architectural impact; C misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single response the citizen-facing benefits assistant produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for public-sector AI systems.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.
This approach is required by FedRAMP regardless of other considerations.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this requirement to FedRAMP, which isn't what the regime mandates.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from citizen-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed if they're observed in production first.
These risks are exclusive to non-government use cases.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: Program staff ask whether the assistant's eligibility-guidance responses could produce disparate outcomes across different applicant demographics.

choices.text: This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final eligibility determinations, not any assistive system.
Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; B and C make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The 25-person engineering team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some staff have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Have each staff member individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes in this FedRAMP context to go through the same review rigor as any other change to an authorized system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for an authorized system.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in an authorized system. A, B, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated data-handling change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.
Disable Claude Code for the team entirely following any incident.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes regardless of relevance.
Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigation.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. C and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly ATO-evidence summary) versus a one-off exploratory coding task.

choices.text: Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time they're needed.
Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. B under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance office wants documented evidence of who accessed what citizen data through the system and when, as part of the ATO evidence package.

choices.text: Access logging is optional if the system has role-based permissions.
Audit logging can be added later without architectural impact.
Only failed access attempts need to be logged.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and C each understate what ATO-grade audit evidence actually requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The steering group for this deployment includes program office, ATO assessors, and engineering stakeholders with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Tailor architectural communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms program-office and ATO-assessor stakeholders can evaluate against their own priorities, not just engineering metrics.
Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders, since they'll relay information to the others.
Skip stakeholder communication until the system is fully built.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences to save effort.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by program-office, assessor, and engineering audiences alike. B, C, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: Midway through the project, eligibility requirements shift meaningfully based on new state regulatory guidance.

choices.text: Refuse to incorporate the change since requirements were already agreed upon.
Incorporate the change silently without informing stakeholders of the impact.

Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders, and adjust the design and timeline accordingly.
Restart the entire project from scratch regardless of the change's actual scope.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally driven requirements shift. A and B mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: After launch, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending once the system passes its ATO assessment.

choices.text: This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration are entirely the operations team's responsibility.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the ATO is granted.
Lifecycle management includes monitoring and iteration based on production signal as part of the architect's ongoing responsibility, not just discovery through authorization.
Monitoring is only necessary if a major incident occurs.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through discovery and authorization. A, B, and D all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: Documentation for this system currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: This level of documentation is sufficient since the "what" is all a future team needs.
Documenting reasoning is unnecessary overhead in a regulated environment.
Documentation should also capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — so a future team can safely extend or modify the system without re-deriving that context.
Only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system, making documentation moot.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system, especially in a regulated context. A, B, and D all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Enablement for a Public-Sector FedRAMP Deployment
questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. You are responsible for governance, ATO-relevant compliance, and developer enablement for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team wants Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting documentation, exploring an unfamiliar module) but is unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves time on every task category by default.

Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction (e.g., repetitive documentation drafting, codebase exploration) versus cases where review overhead may exceed time saved, rather than assuming a blanket benefit.
Mandate Claude Code usage for all tasks regardless of measured benefit.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks without evaluation.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; D forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

questions.scenario_context: The Department of Civic Records Modernization (DCRM), a state-level public-sector agency pursuing a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, is deploying a Claude-powered system that helps citizens navigate benefits applications, alongside a 25-person internal engineering team using Claude Code to build and maintain it. Restrict debugging to a single designated engineer.
The issue can only be resolved by switching to a different tool entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Northfield Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, is building a Claude-powered platform to handle escalated customer contacts — billing disputes, service outages, and retention saves — that its front-line chat system can't resolve. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Northfield's operations stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals Northfield's actual goal is reducing average escalation handle time by 30% with the same headcount, not adding capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since AI projects should aim to create new capability.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction exclusively, regardless of what discovery surfaced.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since the system either works or it doesn't.
Frame the architecture around efficiency, and build success metrics around handle time per agent rather than novel capability.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (less handle time, same headcount) is an efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A, B, and C either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.prompt: Escalation intake, categorization, and routing to the correct back-office queue follow a fixed, well-established sequence of steps that doesn't vary case to case, regardless of dispute type.

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since routing benefits from autonomy regardless of predictability.
A fixed workflow, since the steps are well-defined and don't depend on intermediate findings.
An augmented LLM pattern, since a single enhanced call is sufficient for any escalation workflow.
Whichever pattern is fastest to implement, since the patterns are functionally interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Steps that are well-defined and don't vary case to case are the defining case for a fixed workflow, not autonomous orchestration. A overstates the need for agentic autonomy; C undersells what a genuinely multi-step, standardized process needs; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (billing-dispute analysis, outage diagnostics, retention-offer calculation, resolution drafting).

choices.text: Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
Let each subagent communicate results directly to whichever subagent needs them next, to minimize hops.
Merge all four responsibilities into one subagent to avoid coordination overhead.
Let subagents communicate directly, but log the traffic for later review.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. B and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; C discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent specifically for edge cases.
Add a prompt instruction telling subagents to flag cases they don't recognize.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so they can handle any case type.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers all escalation categories, including retention and legal-threat cases, rather than tuning the existing subagents.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole escalation categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. A, B, and C all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

Business value pillars are a sales concern, not an architectural one.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

Ignore the sentiment since it's not a technical requirement.
Proceed with the technical design and let change management handle it separately with no architectural input.
Recommend against the project entirely based on the sentiment.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. A and B withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

Add a feedback loop capturing offer acceptance and churn outcomes as a first-class architectural component, so the system can improve post-deployment.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures offer acceptance and churn outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment. A, B, and C all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

This cannot be built with Claude at all, since it doesn't involve an agent.
An augmented LLM pattern (a single call enhanced with retrieval/tools) fits this simpler augmentation need without the overhead of agentic orchestration.

choices.text: This has no architectural downside as long as the subagent's prompt is well-written.
More tools always improve a subagent's flexibility and should be encouraged.
This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; the unrelated tools should be removed or moved to a more appropriate subagent.
The fix is to increase the subagent's context window.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not just writing around it. A and B ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

Run outage diagnostics and retention-offer calculation as independent, parallel subagent calls once categorization completes, rather than sequentially.

Combine outage diagnostics and retention-offer calculation into a single subagent to avoid the sequencing question.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (categorization) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. Present the full technical architecture diagram with no simplification.
Skip a high-level description and go directly into an implementation demo.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; C is too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Planner questions range from simple SKU lookups to complex multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis requiring deep reasoning.

choices.text: Always use the highest-capability tier for every query regardless of complexity.
Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple SKU lookups, a balanced tier for typical planning questions, and a higher-capability tier reserved for complex multi-region tradeoff analysis.
Use one fixed mid-tier model for all queries regardless of complexity.
Always use the fastest/cheapest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex analysis.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and D ignore or sacrifice fit-to-task; C forces one tier onto queries with very different needs.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (merchandising rules, tone, formatting) followed by retrieved sales-data excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved content after it, to reduce both latency and cost across the high query volume.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.
Put retrieved content first since it's most relevant to the specific query.
Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. B, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form vendor contracts with short structured SKU/price tables.

choices.text: One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well.
Structured data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and C ignore this mismatch; B discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Planner queries range from exact lookups ("current price for SKU 48213") to conceptual questions ("how has our outdoor-furniture assortment mix shifted over two years").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and C force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Planners need each pricing recommendation reliably mapped to its specific source (vendor contract clause, sales report section), and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without further structure.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible source for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted documents at the end of each response.
Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (document, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. A, B, and C all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two systems disagree on the current on-hand inventory count for a SKU by a meaningful margin — likely due to a stale nightly sync in one of them.

choices.text: Average the two figures and present the average.
Present both figures explicitly annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely explanation (e.g., a stale sync), rather than silently picking one.
Always prefer whichever source was retrieved first.
Omit the inventory figure entirely since sources disagree.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and a likely explanation preserves the actual information for the planner rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. A, C, and D all discard or obscure a genuine data conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with source fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.
Post-process every response to strip leading text before the first `{`.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; B doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary vendor-catalog system, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just the merchandising copilot.

choices.text: Build an MCP server exposing the vendor-catalog operations as tools/resources, reusable across the multiple internal tools that need it.
Hard-code the vendor-catalog integration into this copilot's application code only.
Paste the entire vendor catalog into every prompt.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. B, C, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full vendor catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Progressive discovery (querying a catalog resource as needed) scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the catalog grows.
Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with catalog growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. B and C ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; D removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. questions.prompt: A planner asks a question requiring the model to reason step by step across several sales reports before concluding on an assortment recommendation.

choices.text: A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-document synthesis question.
Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple documents regardless of prompting approach.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (formatting rules, disclaimer language, tone) across several different planner-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).
Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Modular prompts are the same thing as prompt caching.
Standardization across features isn't achievable with prompt design.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. B reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-formatted answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific figure from the correctly retrieved source document.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
Apply defensive validation — verify extracted figures against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C doesn't address correctness; D incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether planner-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the copilot.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Home Goods wants Claude to help merchandising planners answer questions ranging from simple SKU price lookups to complex, multi-region assortment tradeoff analysis, using retrieval over vendor contracts, sales reports, and inventory data. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.

Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; B over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.prompt: The copilot's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/formatting rules and the retrieved excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and D all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.
