questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only flag precision and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Precision alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — a system that flags fraud well but is too slow, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it flags fraud well. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past transactions.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new triage-scoring prompt improves flag quality before rolling it out to all traffic.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all traffic immediately and monitor for problems.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A flagged transaction was wrongly cleared as legitimate. Investigation shows the underlying transaction-history data was retrieved correctly, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved data), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This is a retrieval problem; fix the indexing pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. B and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; C avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled transaction-history database migration, the system starts flagging an elevated rate of clean transactions as fraud, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data migration event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since flagging behavior changed.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data migration event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a transaction-history migration.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency of fraud triage but is worried about hurting recall, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the recall bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing recall at unsustainable cost.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "recall at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the recall bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average precision score.

choices.text: A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.

Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-merchant-category or per-transaction-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. A and D accept a monitoring blind spot; B drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting manual review of flagged transactions by 70%, citing a 98% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Proceed with the cut based on the 98% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new triage model improves flag precision, but the team hasn't checked whether it also changed the false-negative rate on sophisticated fraud patterns that should be escalated.

choices.text: Precision improvement alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
False-negative escalation behavior is not something evaluation can measure.
Check the escalation-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated precision improvement could be masking an increase in missed sophisticated fraud.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated precision improvement could mask a worsened escalation failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and D ship without adequate testing; B incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of flagged transactions are technically correctly classified but investigators rate the accompanying explanation as unhelpful.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves ratings.
Ignore investigator ratings in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

Investigate a dimension beyond factual accuracy — e.g., clarity, completeness, or actionability of the explanation — since "correct but unhelpful" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.

questions.explanation: "Correct but unhelpful" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (clarity, completeness, actionability) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and C discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full transaction history plus a large static fraud-policy document on every turn of multi-turn investigator conversations.

choices.text: Apply prompt caching to the static fraud-policy document and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.
Remove the policy document entirely to save tokens.
Full history is always required, so there is no optimization opportunity here.

questions.explanation: Caching the static fraud-policy document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. D denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production system, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a fraud-policy document update — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a triage-explanation output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. B and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the fraud-triage system is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, safety) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.
Use flag precision alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.
A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. B and D oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data flow, retention, and access-logging design in the final week before launch, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: This sequencing carries no risk since compliance can always be added right before launch.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture.
HIPAA, not GDPR, is the relevant regime for a banking client.
GDPR-driven data-minimization, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.

questions.explanation: GDPR-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and B understate real architectural impact; C misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the customer-facing system produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every output is always the correct default for banking AI systems.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive.
This approach is required by GDPR regardless of other considerations.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and C overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this requirement to GDPR, which doesn't mandate it universally.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from customer-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed if they're observed in production first.
These risks are exclusive to non-banking use cases.
A single generic guardrail addresses all three risk types equally well.

Design mitigations for each known failure mode as part of the architecture up front — e.g., grounding/verification for hallucination, input isolation and guardrails for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance team asks whether the system's credit-related outputs could produce disparate outcomes across different demographic groups.

choices.text: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.
This is not an architectural concern; it belongs entirely to legal/compliance review after launch.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
This concern only applies to systems making final credit decisions, not any assistive system.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. B defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some engineers have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Have each engineer individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team/project level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local setup.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of AI tooling adoption.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes in this banking context to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a regulated system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review since it was "written by AI."
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a regulated system.
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than human-written code.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated data-handling change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigation.
Disable Claude Code for the team entirely following any incident.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces/logs to localize the actual failure point.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes regardless of relevance.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly GDPR data-subject-access-request summary report) versus a one-off exploratory coding task.

choices.text: Build both as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time they're needed.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both as MCP servers regardless of reuse profile.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the real business driver is reducing carrier detention and demurrage fees by 30%, not adding capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame around transformation, since AI projects should always aim to add novel capability.
Frame around throughput/efficiency exclusively, regardless of what discovery found.
Skip pillar framing; a working system speaks for itself.
Frame around cost reduction, anchoring both the architecture and success metrics on detention/demurrage fee reduction.

questions.explanation: Discovery pointed to a cost driver (detention/demurrage fees), so the architecture and metrics should be anchored on cost reduction. A and B misname the pillar the discovery actually surfaced; C skips framing that keeps the project aligned to real value.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: Procurement, mode selection, and exception handling each require different steps depending on carrier responses, inventory position, and disruptions discovered mid-shipment.

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since the right steps vary by shipment and depend on intermediate findings.
A fixed workflow, since freight logistics is a standardized process.
An augmented LLM pattern, since one enhanced call suffices for any logistics task.
Whichever pattern is quickest to prototype, since the patterns are interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by shipment and depend on intermediate findings (carrier responses, disruptions) are the defining case for an agentic pattern. B assumes a predictability the scenario lacks; C undersells the orchestration needed; D ignores real tradeoffs between patterns.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: The design has a coordinator delegating to subagents (procurement, routing, exception-handling, customs-compliance). Every subagent works correctly, but shipments requiring both a customs hold and a carrier substitution are never routed to any subagent — they fall through silently.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent specifically for edge cases.
Instruct subagents to flag unfamiliar shipments in their own prompts.
Broaden existing subagents' tool access so any subagent can handle any case.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers compound cases like simultaneous customs holds and carrier substitutions, rather than tuning subagents.

questions.explanation: Whole compound case categories never being routed at all is a coordinator decomposition gap, not a subagent performance issue. A, B, and C all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap in the coordinator's routing logic.

Any automated system inherently demonstrates transformation.
Business value pillars belong to sales, not architecture.
Choose the pillar after launch, based on whichever benefit is easiest to report.

questions.explanation: Naming a specific pillar (efficiency, cost, transformation, SLA) gives both architecture and metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D each skip or defer that framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

Proceed with the design and let change management address it later, entirely outside the architecture.
Recommend cancelling the project based on the sentiment alone.
Treat the sentiment as a real implicit constraint that shapes rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter most.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment from dispatchers is a real implicit constraint shaping rollout sequencing and HITL placement, not noise to dismiss. A and B treat it as out of scope; C overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing the technical case.

Explain the tradeoff explicitly: exception handling requires deeper reasoning over ambiguous, disruptive events, justifying the added cost/latency, while procurement is more routine and better served by a faster tier.
Use the same tier everywhere for simplicity, regardless of task difficulty.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. cost/latency) is the standard for communicating tier decisions to stakeholders. A and B withhold reasoning stakeholders need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase with no current design hooks.

questions.explanation: A first-class feedback loop capturing dispatcher overrides and outcomes is what lets the system improve post-deployment. A, C, and D each treat this component as optional or someone else's responsibility.

This requires a fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. Combine routing and customs-check into a single subagent to avoid the sequencing question.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no shared dependency can run in parallel once their prerequisite (procurement) completes, cutting latency without sacrificing correctness. A and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. Design the current decomposition and tool/subagent boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements.
Build full intermodal-rail support now, guessing at requirements.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most attorney queries are moderately complex research questions; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many cases, and a small fraction are simple citation lookups.

choices.text: Route based on task difficulty — a fast tier for simple citation lookups, a balanced tier for typical research questions, and a higher-capability tier (potentially with extended thinking) reserved for the deep multi-case cases.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question.
Use one fixed model tier for all questions, regardless of complexity.
Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex research questions. B and D ignore fit-to-task; C sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (jurisdiction rules, citation style, formatting requirements) followed by retrieved case excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable prompt caching, with the varying retrieved excerpts after it, to reduce both latency and cost across the high query volume.
Put retrieved excerpts first since they're most relevant to the specific query.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form judicial opinions with short structured data (a table of statute citations and effective dates).

choices.text: One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form opinions can serve both content types equally well.
Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form opinions need different chunking than short structured records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
Structured statute data should be excluded from retrieval entirely.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything to avoid needing multiple strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorney queries range from exact lookups ("cite for Smith v. Jones") to conceptual questions ("how has the reasonable-reliance standard evolved across circuits").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type.
Use only structured/metadata filtering for every query type.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured/metadata filtering for exact citation lookups, embedding similarity search for conceptual questions, and hybrid retrieval where both are needed.
Query pattern doesn't affect which retrieval approach is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and B force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorneys need citations that reliably map each legal claim to a specific case and pincite, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (case name, reporter citation, pincite, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis rather than being reconstructed from memory.
Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without further structure.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible case for each claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted cases at the end of each response.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved cases disagree on how a particular statute of limitations is tolled — likely because they're from different circuits with different precedent.

choices.text: Average the two positions and present a blended rule.
Omit the tolling analysis entirely since sources disagree.
Always prefer whichever case was retrieved first.
Present both positions explicitly, attributed to their respective circuits, rather than silently picking one or blending them.

questions.explanation: Presenting both positions with attribution preserves the actual information for the attorney rather than resolving a genuine jurisdictional conflict arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard or obscure a real disagreement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction more emphatically in the prompt.
Increase max_tokens to leave room for both the preamble and the JSON.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.
Post-process every response to strip leading text before the first `{`.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and D are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; B doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal brief bank, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

choices.text: Hard-code the brief-bank integration into this platform's application code only.
Paste the entire brief bank into every prompt.
Build an MCP server exposing the brief-bank operations as tools/resources, reusable across the multiple internal Claude-powered tools that need it.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own integration independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, B, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates between exposing the full case-law catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Loading the full catalog up front is always preferable for completeness.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between the two approaches.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form.
Progressive discovery (querying a catalog resource as needed) scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the corpus grows.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: An attorney asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved opinions before concluding on a multi-factor test.

choices.text: A chain-of-thought prompting approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning steps, is well suited to this kind of multi-document, multi-factor synthesis question.
Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding tasks.
The model cannot reason across multiple documents regardless of prompting approach.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning across a multi-factor test. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, jurisdiction disclaimers, formatting rules) across several different attorney-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Duplicate the fragments into each feature's prompt independently.
Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability-packaging lever).
Modular prompts are the same thing as prompt caching.
Standardization across features isn't achievable with prompt design.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific holding from the correctly retrieved opinion.

choices.text: Apply defensive validation — verify extracted holdings against the actual source excerpt rather than accepting confident, well-formatted phrasing as proof of accuracy.
Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence of correctness.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no mitigation.
Increase output length so there's more room to be correct.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted holdings against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. B is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; C incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether attorney-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the research platform.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
SLAs are a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading, since behavior can shift across releases even at improved benchmark scores.
Continue floating to latest automatically, since newer is always better.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. B and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; C over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved case excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed analytical answer.

choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other.
This tradeoff only matters for very long documents, never for typical queries.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of input size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only forecast accuracy against actuals and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety/guardrail behavior.

choices.text: Forecast accuracy alone is sufficient since it's the system's primary purpose.
Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — a system that forecasts well but is too slow, too expensive, or unsafe still fails overall.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it forecasts well. A, B, and C each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed set of past quarters' actual outcomes.

choices.text: A single automated method is sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review (sales-manager judgment) for nuanced calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves forecast-narrative quality before rolling it out to all sales reps.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all reps immediately and monitor for problems.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: A forecast narrative is factually wrong about a deal's stage. Investigation shows the CRM data was correct and retrieved properly, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem; fix the indexing pipeline.
This cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different model tier regardless of the specific failure.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved content), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled CRM data-sync refresh, the copilot starts producing confident but incorrect deal-stage references, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since confidence changed.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data-sync event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the context window shrank.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-sync event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and D would not specifically correlate with a CRM data-sync refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting forecast accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation from one another.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications.

Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall monthly average forecast-accuracy score across all sales regions, hiding drift specific to one region.

choices.text: Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-region or per-deal-size breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment even while looking healthy overall.
A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is captured by the eval suite alone.
Monthly granularity is always sufficient regardless of system behavior.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate monthly average can hide, such as region-specific drift. B and D accept a monitoring blind spot; C drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting manager review of flagged low-confidence forecasts by 80%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by region and deal size before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.
Proceed with the cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment.
Manager review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by region and deal size before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves narrative-quality ratings, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate of overconfident forecasts on genuinely volatile deals that should be flagged as uncertain.

choices.text: Check the uncertainty-flagging failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated narrative-quality improvement could be masking an increase in inappropriate overconfidence on volatile deals.
Narrative-quality rating alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change.
Overconfidence behavior is not something evaluation can measure.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact instead of testing beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated narrative-quality improvement could mask a worsened overconfidence failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. B and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of forecasts are numerically accurate but rated as unhelpful by sales managers in feedback surveys.

choices.text: Investigate a dimension beyond numerical accuracy — e.g., actionability, explanation quality, or relevance to the manager's specific pipeline — since "accurate but unhelpful" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Assume the accuracy metric is broken and discard it.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves helpfulness.
Ignore manager feedback scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but unhelpful" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (actionability, explanation quality) rather than a broken accuracy metric. B and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; C assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full deal history plus a large static sales-methodology reference on every turn of multi-turn conversations with reps.

choices.text: This has no optimization opportunity since full history is always required.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost.
Remove the sales-methodology reference entirely to save tokens.
Apply prompt caching to the static methodology reference and consider trimming or summarizing older turns of conversation history to reduce redundant token cost across a multi-turn conversation.

questions.explanation: Caching the static methodology reference and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production copilot, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change.
Observability requires no structure as long as data is retained somewhere.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, quality metrics by segment — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable or actionable on their own.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a specific forecast-quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a CRM schema change — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent change is always the cause.

This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each change independently rather than guessing.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which (if any) caused the regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; C gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a forecast-narrative output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
The reference string needs to be longer.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the sales-forecasting copilot is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.
Use forecast accuracy alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail (accuracy, latency, cost, safety) so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a specific failing area.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.
